To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the familiarity of stimuli is processed in the theta band in parieto-occipital region.
the familiarity of the stimuli is a key element in affective valence and that this familiarity is reflected by the theta frequency band.
the familiarity of stimuli has a strong influence on the processing of affective valence, and that the parietooccitpital region and the theta band play a crucial role in this process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the affective valences of pictures and how the brain responds to the familiarity of the stimuli.
the investigation of affective valence using EEG signals.
the study of the emotional processing of novel and familiar stimuli and the analysis of the most relevant features for the affective valance discrimination in the ERP domain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the familiarity of the stimuli is processed in parietooccippital region and theta frequency band, while the affective valences of the stimuli are processed mainly in the frontal region and in the alpha frequency band.
the familiarity of stimuli does not affect the affective valences elicited in the brain.
the processing of novelty is more related to theta band, while the processing of familiarity is more related to the alpha band.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the processing of emotional information is not a simple process, it is affected by several factors such as the familiarity of the stimuli, and it involves different frequency bands and regions of the brain.
, when processing novel stimuli, the affective valences of the stimuli are processed in the same way than the familiar stimuli.
the familiarity of the stimuli affects the affect processing, and that theta band is especially involved in the affective processing of novelty stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
habituation phenomenon is a relevant factor to be considered when studying emotional processing in the brain.
the familiarity of the stimulus affects the affective processing, and the brain regions and frequency bands involved are different depending on whether the stimulus is familiar or novel.
the familiarity of the stimulus affects the processing of affective valences in the brain, as it has been demonstrated by the different ERPs elicited by novel stimuli and by familiar stimuli.
